title: What does a test check?
summary: Check whether a result matches what should happen.
goals: Compare the result you expected with the result you observed.
setup: We will use one small program throughout this lesson. Its rule is simple: add one to the number it is given.

flow.title: What should happen?
flow.html:
We have a small program with one rule:

Add one to the number you are given.

If we give it 4, it should give back 5.

The answer it should produce is called the expected result.

flow.title: What actually happened?
flow.html:
We tried the same program with 4. This time it gave back 6.

The answer we actually got is called the actual result. Here, the actual result is 6—even though the rule tells us to expect 5.

flow.title: Compare the two results
flow.html:
Now put the two results side by side.

Expected resultActual result
56

They do not match. This check fails.

If the actual result were 5, the two would match and the check would pass. This comparison is the basic idea of a test.

flow.title: Try the same check with another number
flow.html:
Keep the same rule: add one.

This time, give the program 8. It gives back 9.

First work out what it should give back. Then compare that with what it actually gave back.

practice.title: Choose the expected result
practice.prompt: The rule is “add one.” We give the program 6. What result should we expect?

options.feedback: That leaves the number unchanged.
6 plus one is 7. That is the expected result.
That adds two instead of one.

practice.hint: Apply the rule: 6 + 1.

practice.title: Identify the actual result
practice.prompt: The program should add one. We give it 4, and it gives back 6. What is the actual result?

options.feedback: 4 is the number we gave the program.
5 is what we expected, not what we observed.
6 is the result the program actually gave back.

practice.hint: Look for the result we got, even if it was wrong.
practice.solution: The actual result is 6. “Actual” means observed, not necessarily correct.

practice.title: Does this check pass?
practice.prompt: A program should add one. Given 4, its expected result is 5, but its actual result is 6. Write one sentence saying whether this check passes or fails, and why.
practice.hint: Compare 5 with 6.
practice.solution: The check fails because the actual result, 6, does not match the expected result, 5.
rubric: Says the check fails.
Explains that 6 does not match 5.

practice.title: Make the comparison yourself
practice.prompt: The rule is “add one.” We give the program 8, and its actual result is 9. State the expected result, then say whether the check passes or fails.
practice.hint: Work out 8 + 1 before comparing it with 9.
practice.solution: Expected result: 9. The check passes because the actual result is also 9.
rubric: Uses the rule to get an expected result of 9.
Says the check passes because expected and actual match.

bridge: You have compared an expected result with an actual result. Next, we will give this same add-one program a name and read the small Java instruction that asks it to run.

title: Read a call, then check its types
summary: Read one small Java instruction at a time.
goals: Read inputs and the returned type from a method header.
Write a call and store its returned int.
Distinguish int, String, Integer and an absent Integer value.
setup: Continue with the add-one operation. Read one small Java step, then practise that same step.

flow.title: Read one method call
flow.html:
Think of Numbers as a named group of number operations. addOne is one operation in that group. It returns one more than the number you supply. In this call, the dot selects addOne from Numbers, and the parentheses hold its input, 4. The returned number is 5.

Numbers.addOne(4)

flow.title: Distinguish a number from text
flow.html:
addOne expects an int: a whole-number value. The expression 4 is an int, while "4" is a String containing text. The matching digit does not make them the same type. Java rejects the quoted input for this method before the method can run.

Numbers.addOne(4)

flow.title: Read the method header
flow.html:
This header describes the same addOne operation. static lets us call it through the group name Numbers. The int before addOne says the returned result is a whole number. Inside the parentheses, int number says the input is a whole number called number. The header describes the operation; it does not run it.

static int addOne(int number)

flow.title: Store the returned number
flow.html:
A variable gives a value a name. int actual declares a whole-number variable named actual. The = stores the result of the call in it. The semicolon ends the statement. After this statement, actual contains 5 because addOne received 4 and returned one more.

int actual = Numbers.addOne(4);

flow.title: Match two inputs to two slots
flow.html:
Numbers also provides a sum operation with header static int total(int base, int extra). A comma separates its two input slots. The first supplied value goes to base; the second goes to extra. This call gives base the value 4 and extra the value 1, so total returns 5.

Numbers.total(4, 1)

flow.title: Change the second parameter to Integer
flow.html:
We now revise total: its second parameter changes from int extra to Integer extra. Base and the return type remain int. Integer is an object form of a whole number, allowing an optional value. Integer.valueOf(1) supplies an Integer representing one. Use this revised header for the remaining steps.

Numbers.total(4, Integer.valueOf(1))

flow.title: Represent an absent optional value
flow.html:
null means that no Integer object is supplied. The revised total contract says a null extra contributes zero. Therefore the call below returns 4. Null can occupy the Integer slot, but it cannot be passed directly to the int base slot: that slot still requires a whole-number value.

Numbers.total(4, null)

flow.title: Let Java box the argument
flow.html:
Java can convert an int argument into Integer when the parameter requires Integer. This automatic conversion is called boxing. In the call below, base receives the int 4. The second int, 1, is automatically wrapped for extra. The result is still 5; you have shortened the way the second argument is written.

Numbers.total(4, 1)

flow.title: Recognize unboxing and a missing value
flow.html:
The reverse conversion, from Integer to int, is unboxing. Inside total, this statement asks for the number held by extra. It compiles. If extra is null, however, there is no number to extract: execution stops with NullPointerException. To meet the null-means-zero contract, total must handle that case before trying to unbox it.

int copiedExtra = extra;

practice.title: Find the supplied input
practice.prompt: Numbers.addOne returns one more than the supplied number. In Numbers.addOne(4), which part is the input value?

options.feedback: The value inside the parentheses is the input supplied to addOne.
Numbers names the group containing the operation.
addOne names the operation being called.

practice.hint: Look inside the parentheses.

practice.title: Choose the required type
practice.prompt: Numbers.addOne requires an int input. Which call supplies the whole-number value four in that type?

options.feedback: The unquoted 4 is an int value.
The quotes make "4" a String, not an int argument.

practice.hint: Double quotes make a text value.

practice.title: Identify the returned type
practice.prompt:
Read this header from Numbers. Which part says what type of result the method returns?

static int addOne(int number)

options.feedback: That position declares the return type.
number names the input parameter inside the parentheses.
Numbers identifies the group containing the method, not its returned type.

practice.hint: The returned type appears before the method name.
practice.solution: The int immediately before addOne declares the returned type.

practice.title: Write one storing statement
practice.prompt: Numbers provides static int addOne(int number), returning one more than its input. Write one statement that calls it with 7 and stores the returned result in an int variable named actual. Use the method call, rather than writing its answer directly.
practice.hint: Use the pattern: int variableName = methodCall;
practice.solution:
int actual = Numbers.addOne(7);

The statement stores the returned value 8 in actual.
rubric: Declares int actual.
Calls Numbers.addOne(7).
Assigns the returned result and ends the statement with a semicolon.

practice.title: Match the input order
practice.prompt: Numbers currently provides static int total(int base, int extra), returning base plus extra. For Numbers.total(4, 1), which parameter receives the value 4?

options.feedback: base is the first parameter, so it receives the first supplied value.
extra is second and receives 1 in this call.
Each supplied value goes to its corresponding parameter slot.

practice.hint: Match positions from left to right.

practice.title: Supply the revised parameter type
practice.prompt: The revised header is static int total(int base, Integer extra) in Numbers. It adds the supplied values. Which call explicitly supplies an Integer representing 1 for extra, while supplying the int value 4 for base?

options.feedback: Integer.valueOf(1) supplies the Integer value for the second slot.
The second argument is a String, not an Integer.
The second argument fits, but the first is a String where base requires int.

practice.hint: Keep base as an int and use Integer.valueOf for extra.

practice.title: Leave only extra absent
practice.prompt: Numbers provides static int total(int base, Integer extra). It returns base plus extra, treating a null extra as zero. Which call correctly supplies base 4 and no Integer object for extra?

options.feedback: The int base is 4 and the nullable Integer slot receives null; the result is 4.
The null literal cannot be supplied directly to the int base parameter.
The optional value is absent, but the first argument is a String rather than an int.

practice.hint: The optional Integer is the second parameter.
practice.solution:
Numbers.total(4, null)

The contract requires the returned value 4.

practice.title: Simplify the explicit conversion
practice.prompt:
Numbers provides static int total(int base, Integer extra). Rewrite this call using automatic int-to-Integer boxing for extra. Preserve the input values and end your statement with a semicolon.

Numbers.total(7, Integer.valueOf(2));
practice.hint: The Integer parameter lets Java box an int argument automatically.
practice.solution:
Numbers.total(7, 2);

Base receives 7. Java boxes 2 for the Integer extra parameter. The returned sum is 9.
rubric: Keeps Numbers.total and the two inputs in the same order.
Replaces Integer.valueOf(2) with the int expression 2.
Ends the call statement with a semicolon.

practice.title: Explain what happens before a result is returned
practice.prompt:
Numbers provides static int total(int base, Integer extra), promising that null extra contributes zero. A caller uses Numbers.total(4, null). A proposed implementation begins with this statement. Does the statement fail to compile, or fail when it runs? Name the operation responsible and explain whether it meets the promised null behaviour.

int copiedExtra = extra;
practice.hint: The declared Integer type can be unboxed, but the current value is null.
practice.solution: The statement compiles, then throws NullPointerException while unboxing the null extra. It does not store an int in copiedExtra or produce the promised total of 4. The implementation must handle the absent extra as zero before attempting to extract an int from it.
rubric: Says the statement compiles.
Identifies runtime NullPointerException caused by unboxing null.
Explains that the promised null-as-zero behaviour has not been implemented.

teachBack.prompt: In the revised total method, why can extra be null while base cannot be supplied as null?
teachBack.answer: Extra has type Integer, which can represent an absent object. Base has type int and requires a whole-number value. The contract says an absent extra contributes zero; extracting an int from null without handling that case throws NullPointerException.

bridge: Next, practise building the exact values that other method parameters require.

title: Build the values a method needs
summary: Create one value or object at a time, then read what its operations accept and return.
goals: Construct the value or object required by a parameter.
Distinguish an object’s state, an instance call, and a static call.
Read String, char, array, boolean, and BigInteger values.
setup: Create one value or object at a time, then read what its operations accept and return.

flow.title: A class and one of its objects
flow.html:
Numbers gave us a named group of operations. A Java class can also describe objects we create. We will use a supplied class named Counter. Each Counter object holds its own whole-number count. The class describes the kind of object; an instance is one particular object made from that description.

NameMeaning
CounterThe class
One Counter objectAn instance with its own count

flow.title: Create an object with new
flow.html:
The expression new Counter() creates a fresh Counter starting at zero. A constructor initializes the new object. This one takes no inputs, so its parentheses are empty. The whole statement gives the object the variable name counter. Its variable type is Counter, matching the object it refers to.

Counter counter = new Counter();

flow.title: Read an object’s stored state
flow.html:
A value stored inside an object is a field. The values currently stored in its fields are its state. Counter stores one count. Its supplied method int get() returns that count. Calling counter.get() reads the state of the object named counter. Empty parentheses mean this call supplies no arguments.

Counter counter = new Counter();
int actual = counter.get();

flow.title: Choose the receiver of an instance call
flow.html:
A static operation such as Numbers.addOne is called through its class name. An instance operation such as get is called on a particular object. That object is the call’s receiver. Use the variable counter to read its count; the class name Counter does not select an individual object’s stored state.

Numbers.addOne(4);
counter.get();

flow.title: A void operation changes state
flow.html:
Counter also supplies void set(int next). For the nonnegative inputs used here, it replaces the stored count with next. void means the call returns no value. Perform the update as its own statement, then call get to observe the new count. Do not try to store a returned number from set: there is no returned number.

Counter counter = new Counter();
counter.set(4);
int actual = counter.get();

flow.title: A boolean answers a yes-or-no question
flow.html:
A boolean has exactly two possible values: true and false. For this example Counter supplies boolean isZero(), which returns true when its stored count is zero and false otherwise. This is a different return type from get. Store its result in a boolean variable because the observation is a yes-or-no answer.

Counter counter = new Counter();
boolean actual = counter.isZero();

flow.title: Store a String value
flow.html:
A String is an object representing text. Double quotes write a String value in Java. Just as int actual names a whole-number value, String name names a String reference. The empty String is written as two adjacent quotes: it is real text with zero characters, rather than an absent object.

String name = "Ada";
String empty = "";

flow.title: Call an operation on a String
flow.html:
A String has instance operations too. Its method int length() returns its length. In these examples each ordinary letter occupies one position, so cat has length three. The receiver text identifies which String to measure. The parentheses remain empty because the String itself supplies the text being measured.

String text = "cat";
int actual = text.length();

flow.title: Distinguish char from String
flow.html:
Single quotes write a char value, such as 'A'. Double quotes write a String, such as "A". Even when both show one letter, they are different Java types. A parameter declared String needs a String expression; Java does not automatically turn a char argument into a String for that call.

char letter = 'A';
String text = "A";

flow.title: Ask whether String contents match
flow.html:
The String operation equals compares text contents and returns a boolean. For a non-null receiver text, text.equals("cat") asks whether its contents are cat. This combines the two types you just learned: the receiver is a String object, while the result of the comparison is a boolean.

String text = "cat";
boolean sameText = text.equals("cat");

flow.title: Create an array of int values
flow.html:
An array holds an ordered sequence of values of one element type. The type int[] means an array of ints. In new int[]{2, 5}, the braces list the elements in order. The variable values refers to one array object containing those two numbers; it is not itself one int.

int[] values = new int[]{2, 5};

flow.title: Read an array element by index
flow.html:
An index selects an array position. Java starts numbering positions at zero. For the array below, index 0 contains 2 and index 1 contains 5. Square brackets after the variable read the selected element. The result has the element type int, rather than the array type int[].

int[] values = new int[]{2, 5};
int second = values[1];

flow.title: Read an array’s length
flow.html:
An array exposes a field named length containing its element count. Read it without parentheses. An array of length two has indexes 0 and 1, so its length is not a valid last index. The expression new int[0] creates an empty array with length zero; the array still exists.

int[] values = new int[]{2, 5};
int count = values.length;

flow.title: Import a library class name
flow.html:
Some useful classes come from Java’s libraries. A package is a named group of classes and related types. An import lets you use a short class name instead of its full package-qualified name. The line below makes BigInteger available by its short name. Imports belong at the top of a source file, before its class declaration.

import java.math.BigInteger;

flow.title: Construct a BigInteger argument
flow.html:
BigInteger is another class representing integer values, including values larger than int can hold. It is different from the Integer wrapper. Its static operation BigInteger.valueOf(5) supplies a BigInteger representing five. A parameter requiring BigInteger needs that object form; the int-to-Integer boxing rule does not turn 5 into BigInteger.

BigInteger amount = BigInteger.valueOf(5);

flow.title: Keep numeric zero separate from null
flow.html:
BigInteger provides a named value BigInteger.ZERO, an object representing numeric zero. This is different from null, which represents no object. Both expressions can fit a BigInteger reference slot, but the contract can treat them differently. Constructing the correct type comes first; choosing an allowed value is the next decision.

BigInteger zero = BigInteger.ZERO;
BigInteger absent = null;

practice.title: A class and one of its objects
practice.prompt: Counter is a class describing objects that each hold a count. Which phrase describes an instance?
practice.hint: Separate the description from one object made from it.
practice.solution: An instance is one particular Counter object.

options.feedback: An instance is an individual object of the class.

options.text: The description of every Counter object
options.feedback: That describes the class, rather than one instance.

practice.title: Create an object with new
practice.prompt: The supplied no-argument constructor Counter() creates a Counter starting at zero. Write one statement creating a Counter variable named first.
practice.hint: Follow: ClassName variableName = new ClassName();
rubric: Declares a Counter variable named first.
Uses new Counter() with empty parentheses.
Assigns the new object and ends with a semicolon.

practice.title: Read an object’s stored state
practice.prompt:
new Counter() starts with count zero, and int get() returns that count. What value does actual contain?

Counter counter = new Counter();
int actual = counter.get();
practice.hint: Read the constructor’s starting state, then the getter’s promise.

options.feedback: The new Counter stores zero, and get returns it.
get returns an int count, not the object.
The documented return type is int and the current count is zero.

practice.title: Choose the receiver of an instance call
practice.prompt: A Counter object is stored in counter. Its method int get() is an instance method. Which call reads that object’s count?
practice.hint: An instance call needs the variable referring to the object.

options.feedback: counter identifies the instance whose count is read.
get is not static; the class name does not supply an instance.

practice.title: A void operation changes state
practice.prompt: Counter starts at zero. void set(int next) replaces its count, and int get() returns the current count. Starting with Counter counter = new Counter();, write two statements that set the count to 7 and store the observed count in int actual.
practice.hint: First change the state; then use the method that returns a value.
rubric: Calls counter.set(7) as a statement.
Reads counter.get() afterward.
Stores that returned int in actual.

practice.title: A boolean answers a yes-or-no question
practice.prompt:
Counter starts at zero. Its supplied boolean isZero() returns true exactly when the count is zero. What does this fragment store in actual?

Counter counter = new Counter();
counter.set(3);
boolean actual = counter.isZero();
practice.hint: Answer the yes-or-no question, not the count question.

options.feedback: The stored count is 3, so it is not zero.
That would be the count returned by get; isZero returns a boolean.
isZero is true only for the stored count zero.

practice.title: Store a String value
practice.prompt: Write one statement declaring a String variable named name containing the text Lin.
practice.hint: Use the same declaration-and-assignment shape as an int variable.
rubric: Uses the type String.
Names the variable name.
Uses the double-quoted value "Lin" and a semicolon.

practice.title: Call an operation on a String
practice.prompt:
For the ordinary letters used here, String.length() returns the number of letters. Write the value stored in actual and identify its type.

String text = "fish";
int actual = text.length();
practice.hint: Do not confuse the receiver’s type with the method’s returned type.
practice.solution: The value is 4 and its type is int. The String has four letters, and length() returns an int.
rubric: Gives the value 4.
Identifies int as the returned/stored type.

practice.title: Distinguish char from String
practice.prompt: The only method is static int lengthOf(String text) in TextRules. Which call supplies a one-letter String?
practice.hint: Check the quote marks, not just the displayed letter.

options.feedback: Double quotes produce the required String.
Single quotes produce char, which does not match the String parameter.

practice.title: Ask whether String contents match
practice.prompt:
String.equals compares text contents. What is stored in sameText?

String text = "cat";
boolean sameText = text.equals("dog");
practice.hint: Compare the actual letters, not only the length.

options.feedback: cat and dog have different contents.
Equal length alone does not make String contents equal.
equals returns a boolean; length() is the operation returning a count.

practice.title: Create an array of int values
practice.prompt: Write one statement creating an int-array variable named values with elements 4, 8, and 9 in that order.
practice.hint: Use new int[]{...} to list the elements.
rubric: Uses int[] as the variable type.
Names the variable values.
Creates the elements 4, 8, 9 in that order.

practice.title: Read an array element by index
practice.prompt: Java array indexes start at zero. For int[] values = new int[]{4, 8, 9};, which expression reads 8?
practice.hint: Count positions as 0, 1, 2.

options.feedback: 8 is in the second position, whose index is 1.
Index 0 contains 4.
Index 2 contains 9.

practice.title: Read an array’s length
practice.prompt:
Arrays expose an int field named length. What does each expression produce? Write both counts.

new int[]{4, 8, 9}.length
new int[0].length
practice.hint: Length counts elements rather than giving the last index.
practice.solution: The first length is 3; the second is 0. The second expression creates an existing array containing no elements.
rubric: Gives 3 for the three-element array.
Gives 0 for the empty array.

practice.title: Import a library class name
practice.prompt: BigInteger belongs to the package java.math. Write the import that allows the short name BigInteger in a source file.
practice.hint: The package name comes before the class name.
rubric: Uses import followed by java.math.BigInteger.
Ends the import with a semicolon.

practice.title: Construct a BigInteger argument
practice.prompt: BigInteger is imported. A method void setAmount(BigInteger amount) belongs to an existing object named store. Which call supplies a BigInteger representing 5?
practice.hint: Use the class whose type the parameter requires.

options.feedback: valueOf supplies the required BigInteger value.
The int literal is not automatically converted to BigInteger.
A String containing digits is not a BigInteger.

practice.title: Keep numeric zero separate from null
practice.prompt: BigInteger is imported. A method requires a BigInteger representing numeric zero. Write one suitable argument expression, then explain why null would not express that value.
practice.hint: Zero is a numeric value; null describes a reference.
practice.solution:
BigInteger.ZERO

It represents the number zero. Null represents an absent object, not a zero-valued BigInteger. BigInteger.valueOf(0) is another valid expression.
rubric: Uses BigInteger.ZERO or BigInteger.valueOf(0).
Distinguishes a zero-valued object from an absent reference.

bridge: You can now supply and observe several kinds of values. Next, read the statements inside a method and follow them in order.

title: Follow the statements inside a method
summary: Trace one statement, decision, or loop at a time.
goals: Track variables through assignments and returns.
Read comparisons, branches, and short-circuit expressions.
Trace loops and identify when a return exits the method.
setup: Trace one statement, decision, or loop at a time.

flow.title: Read a method body and its return
flow.html:
A method header describes its name and types. The statements inside its braces form the body: the work performed when it is called. A return statement ends the call and supplies its result. Here number + 1 calculates one more than the supplied number, matching the add-one operation you already know.

static int addOne(int number) {
    return number + 1;
}

flow.title: Update an existing variable
flow.html:
The first statement below creates result. The next updates the existing variable, without repeating its type. Java reads the right side first, then stores that value on the left. With number equal to 4, result changes from 4 to 5. The compact form result += 1; means the same as result = result + 1;.

int result = number;
result = result + 1;
return result;

flow.title: Compare equality without assigning
flow.html:
One equals sign assigns a value. For ints, two equals signs, ==, ask whether their numeric values are equal and produce a boolean. The operator != asks whether they differ. These comparisons do not change the compared values. Later, you will distinguish comparing object references from comparing object contents.

int number = 4;
boolean isFour = number == 4;
boolean isDifferent = number != 4;

flow.title: Read inclusive and strict comparisons
flow.html:
The operators < and > mean less than and greater than. Adding an equals sign includes equality: <= and >=. At the exact compared value, that extra equality matters. Each comparison returns a boolean without changing the numbers. Here strict is false and inclusive is true.

boolean strict = 4 < 4;
boolean inclusive = 4 <= 4;

flow.title: Take an if branch
flow.html:
An if tests a boolean condition. When true, Java runs its block; when false, Java skips it. Here a negative input returns zero immediately; a nonnegative input reaches the final return. A one-statement if can omit its braces, so if (number < 0) return 0; has the same meaning.

static int nonnegative(int number) {
    if (number < 0) {
        return 0;
    }
    return number;
}

flow.title: Choose the alternative with else
flow.html:
An else supplies the alternative block when an if condition is false. Exactly one of these two blocks runs for a call. This version of nonnegative expresses the same two cases explicitly: return zero for a negative input, otherwise return the input itself.

static int nonnegative(int number) {
    if (number < 0) {
        return 0;
    } else {
        return number;
    }
}

flow.title: Require both conditions with &&
flow.html:
The operator && means both conditions must be true. This expression asks whether number is at least 1 and at most 3. With number equal to 2, both comparisons are true. With number equal to 4, the upper comparison is false, so the combined answer is false.

boolean allowed = number >= 1 && number <= 3;

flow.title: Allow either condition with ||
flow.html:
The operator || means at least one condition must be true. This expression asks whether number lies below 1 or above 3. A value on either outside side makes it true. A value inside the range makes both comparisons false, so the combined result is false.

boolean outside = number < 1 || number > 3;

flow.title: See when && skips the right side
flow.html:
Java evaluates && from left to right. If the left condition is false, the whole answer is already false, so Java skips the right condition. This is called short-circuiting. In the expression below, a null text makes the left side false and prevents calling length on an absent String.

boolean hasText = text != null && text.length() > 0;

flow.title: See when || skips the right side
flow.html:
For ||, a true left condition is already enough to make the answer true. Java therefore skips the right condition in that case. With null text below, the left side is true and length is not called. With non-null text, the left side is false and Java must evaluate the right side.

boolean missing = text == null || text.length() == 0;

flow.title: Repeat with while
flow.html:
A while loop checks its condition before each repetition. If true, it runs the body and checks again. If false, it continues after the loop. Here the update increases count each time. The loop visits counts 0, 1, and 2, then stops when count reaches 3.

int count = 0;
while (count < 3) {
    count = count + 1;
}

flow.title: Recognize zero loop iterations
flow.html:
A while body does not have to run even once. If its condition is false on the first check, Java skips the body entirely. This gives a useful reading habit: inspect the initial values before predicting any updates. In the example below, count starts at the stopping value and stays there.

int count = 3;
while (count < 3) {
    count = count + 1;
}

flow.title: Read one-step updates
flow.html:
When used as its own statement, count++; increases count by one. Similarly, count--; decreases it by one. These are compact versions of the updates you already traced. We use them only as standalone updates here, so focus on how the stored value changes after the statement.

count++;
count--;

flow.title: Read the three parts of for
flow.html:
A for loop puts initialization, condition, and update together. Initialization runs once. The condition is checked before each body execution. The update runs after each completed body. In this example i starts at zero, the body runs for i equal to 0 and 1, and then the condition becomes false.

int visits = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++) {
    visits = visits + 1;
}

flow.title: Trace an array loop
flow.html:
Combine the loop with array indexes you already know. The length gives the stopping value; values[i] supplies the current element. total starts at zero and accumulates each element in order. For the two-element array below, the body reads index 0 and then index 1, producing total 7.

int[] values = new int[]{2, 5};
int total = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < values.length; i++) {
    total = total + values[i];
}

flow.title: A return also exits a loop’s method
flow.html:
Return ends the entire method, even when it appears inside a loop. This method sums values only until it encounters zero. At zero, it returns the total already accumulated. No later array element is visited. The return after the loop is used when the loop finishes without encountering a zero.

static int beforeZero(int[] values) {
    int total = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < values.length; i++) {
        if (values[i] == 0) return total;
        total = total + values[i];
    }
    return total;
}

bridge: You can trace what an implementation does. Next, read its written promises so you can decide what it should do.

title: Read what the method promises
summary: Read one part of a written contract before choosing an expected result.
goals: Extract input assumptions, returned results, and state changes.
Distinguish documented rejection from unspecified behavior.
Use the contract as the basis for an expected result.
setup: Read one part of a written contract before choosing an expected result.

flow.title: A comment describes a promise
flow.html:
Text after // is a comment lasting to the end of its line. Java does not execute it. A comment can describe the behavior a method should provide. Read that promise before inspecting the body: a body can contain a defect, so its current result is not automatically the correct expected result.

// Returns one more than number.
static int addOne(int number)

flow.title: Recognize a Javadoc comment
flow.html:
A comment beginning with /** and ending with */ is a Javadoc comment. It can span several lines and describe the method below it. The opening and closing marks belong to the comment, not to the method’s executable body. Here the signature is shown without its body so you can focus on the promise.

/**
 * Returns one more than number.
 */
static int addOne(int number)

flow.title: Read the parameter description
flow.html:
The Javadoc tag @param names a parameter and explains its role. The header still determines the Java type. In this excerpt, number is the input to increase. The description helps you choose meaningful values, while int number tells you that the argument must fit the int slot.

/**
 * @param number the whole number to increase
 */
static int addOne(int number)

flow.title: Read the returned-result description
flow.html:
The Javadoc tag @return describes the result of normal completion. The type int only says what kind of value comes back; this description tells you which int is required. For number equal to 4, the phrase number plus one gives an expected result of 5.

/** @return number plus one */
static int addOne(int number)

flow.title: Read a precondition
flow.html:
A precondition states an assumption the caller must satisfy. This new method, nextDigit, promises a result only when its input is from 0 through 8. The excerpt gives no rule for other inputs. You can state the expected result for 4, but you cannot invent a required result for 9.

/** Requires digit from 0 through 8. Returns digit plus one. */
static int nextDigit(int digit)

flow.title: Read a documented exception
flow.html:
A contract can explicitly describe rejection instead of leaving it unspecified. The tag @throws names an exception and the condition that requires it. An exception is an exceptional completion rather than an ordinary returned value. For this checkedCount method, a negative input must produce IllegalArgumentException; it must not quietly return a count.

/**
 * Returns count when count is nonnegative.
 * @throws IllegalArgumentException if count is negative
 */
static int checkedCount(int count)

flow.title: Read a state-change promise
flow.html:
Not every promise describes a return value. Counter’s void set(int next) replaces its stored count. Because the call returns nothing, observe the effect through int get(). If the count was 3 and set receives 5, the required state afterward is 5. “Replace” does not mean add to the old value.

counter.set(5);
int actual = counter.get();

flow.title: Read what must remain unchanged
flow.html:
A rejection contract can promise both an exception and unchanged state. Suppose Counter.set rejects negative values with IllegalArgumentException and leaves its old count intact. Starting from 3, a rejected set(-1) must still leave 3. Those are two observations of one rejected operation, not two different input cases.

OperationRequired observations
set(-1) when the count is 3IllegalArgumentException; count remains 3

flow.title: Leave unspecified details unspecified
flow.html:
A contract may specify an exception type without specifying its exact message. In that case, requiring one particular sentence adds a rule the API never promised. The same principle applies to internal field names or an unstated selection order. Base each expectation on something the contract actually says.

/** @throws IllegalArgumentException if count is negative */
static int checkedCount(int count)

flow.title: Extract a small contract yourself
flow.html:
Bring the pieces together using a familiar String operation. The header gives the input and return types. The comment assigns a result to null and a result to every non-null String. Derive each observation directly from those rules. No implementation body is needed to decide the expected results for these simple cases.

/** Returns 0 for null; otherwise returns text.length(). */
static int lengthOrZero(String text)

practice.prompt: A Counter currently stores 3. Its void set(int next) replaces the count, and int get() reads it. After counter.set(5), what should get return, and why?

practice.prompt: Counter.set(int) rejects a negative argument with IllegalArgumentException and preserves the previous count. A counter starts this call with count 6. List both required observations for counter.set(-2).
practice.hint: Read both the rejection and preservation promises.

practice.hint: Find a sentence supporting the expectation.
practice.solution: The specified exception type is justified; the invented message and field name are not.

options.feedback: The contract explicitly names that type.

options.feedback: No exact message was specified.

options.feedback: The contract says nothing about that representation.

practice.prompt: Names provides static int lengthOrZero(String text). Its contract returns 0 for null and otherwise returns text.length(). Give the parameter type, return type, expected result for null, and expected result for "cat".
practice.hint: Use the null rule for one case and the length rule for the other.

bridge: You can read the promise. Next, turn one promise at a time into a concrete starting state, input, and expected observation.

title: Build one concrete test case
summary: Choose the starting situation, the input, and the expected observation before writing a test.
goals: Describe a case using setup, input, and expected behavior.
Choose values on and beside a stated boundary.
Isolate one invalid input while keeping the other inputs valid.
setup: Choose the starting situation, the input, and the expected observation before writing a test.

flow.title: Write an input and its expected result
flow.html:
A concrete case names an input and the required observation. “Test addOne” does not yet tell someone what to try or what should happen. “Call addOne with 4 and expect 5” does. Start with this small pair before worrying about Java test syntax. The expected value comes from the add-one promise.

CallExpected result
Numbers.addOne(4)5

flow.title: Include the starting state
flow.html:
For an object operation, the starting state is part of the case. Counter starts at zero; set replaces its count and get reads it. To check replacement of an existing nonzero value, first establish 3, then perform the set being tested. Keep that setup distinct from the target operation.

Counter counter = new Counter();
counter.set(3);
counter.set(5);

flow.title: Choose the expectation independently
flow.html:
The implementation under test may be wrong. Do not obtain the expected answer by calling that same implementation again. Use the written rule or a hand-worked small case. For addOne(4), the expected value is 5 even if the current implementation repeatedly returns 6.

Independent expected valueObserved result
4 plus 1 = 5Whatever this invocation returns

flow.title: Pick an ordinary valid case
flow.html:
We now use a different supplied method, Levels.allowed. It returns true for levels 1 through 3 inclusive and false otherwise. The technique is unchanged: choose a concrete input and apply the rule. Level 2 is an ordinary interior case because it lies strictly between the accepted endpoints.

static boolean allowed(int level)

flow.title: Test the lower endpoint
flow.html:
An inclusive endpoint belongs to the accepted range. For Levels.allowed, level 1 is accepted. The nearest integer below it is 0, which is rejected. These two cases are useful because a mistaken comparison that excludes equality would change the answer at 1 while leaving many ordinary cases unchanged.

LevelExpected
0false
1true

flow.title: Test the upper endpoint
flow.html:
Use the same reasoning at the other end. Level 3 is the last accepted integer. Level 4 is the first rejected integer above it. Testing exactly 3 distinguishes an inclusive upper comparison from one that stops too early. Testing 4 checks that acceptance does not extend beyond the stated range.

LevelExpected
3true
4false

flow.title: Give each selected case a reason
flow.html:
Combine your boundary cases into a small table. The purpose column explains why each row belongs. It helps you notice when many rows merely repeat one interior situation. This table is useful evidence about the endpoints; it is not a claim that every possible implementation defect has been ruled out.

InputExpectedPurpose
0falseJust below the range
1trueFirst accepted level
3trueLast accepted level
4falseJust above the range

flow.title: Keep the other argument valid
flow.html:
A new method, Bookings.accepts(int count, String name), accepts counts 1 through 3 with any non-null name. It returns false otherwise. To check the null-name rule, keep count valid. Then a rejection cannot be explained merely by an invalid count. This isolates the particular restriction you want to investigate.

Target restrictionArgumentsExpected
Null name2, nullfalse

flow.title: Explain a masked check
flow.html:
Suppose Bookings.accepts accidentally ignores name. The call accepts(0, null) would still return false because the count is outside 1–3. That passing result would not establish that null names are checked. A better witness keeps count inside the accepted range while changing only the name to null.

Bookings.accepts(0, null)

flow.title: Plan a case without JUnit yet
flow.html:
Finish by writing the whole experiment in plain language. Keep the starting state, target call, observation, and expected value separate. For Counter.set, the target operation returns void, so observe get afterward. This plan will become a small JUnit test next; the reasoning does not depend on memorizing assertion names.

PartQuestion
SetupWhat state exists before the target call?
ActionWhich call is being checked?
ObservationWhat can you read afterward?
ExpectedWhat does the contract require?

bridge: You can now choose and explain a case. Next, express its expected-versus-actual comparison using JUnit.

title: Build your first JUnit test
summary: Write the comparison, then build its surrounding test structure one piece at a time.
goals: Write an equality assertion using an independent expected value.
Construct a valid ordinary JUnit Jupiter test method.
Assemble its class and imports into a complete test file.
setup: Write the comparison, then build its surrounding test structure one piece at a time.

flow.title: Write an equality assertion
flow.html:
JUnit is a library for running tests. Its operation assertEquals compares an expected value with an actual value. Put expected first and actual second. The comma separates them; the semicolon ends the statement. If the values differ, JUnit reports a failed assertion. Start with this one statement before building its surrounding file.

assertEquals(5, 5);

flow.title: Keep expected and actual in order
flow.html:
The first argument is the answer required by the contract. The second is the observation being checked. Reversing them can still compare equal values, but it reverses the labels in a failure report. Keep their roles explicit so a message saying expected 5 but was 6 accurately describes the experiment.

assertEquals(5, 6);

flow.title: Check the result of the familiar call
flow.html:
Replace the literal actual value with an observation from the method. Numbers.addOne(4) should return 5. The first statement captures whatever it actually returns. The second compares that observation with the independently calculated 5. You have joined the variable statement you learned earlier to the new assertion.

int actual = Numbers.addOne(4);
assertEquals(5, actual);

flow.title: Add a helpful failure message
flow.html:
An equality assertion can take a third argument: a String explaining the expectation if the check fails. It does not change which values are compared. The two numeric arguments still mean expected and actual. Choose a message that identifies the behavior, so the failure tells you what the test was checking.

assertEquals(5, actual, "addOne must increase 4 to 5");

flow.title: Put the statements inside a void method
flow.html:
A test will be a method containing your experiment. This method returns void because it does not return the production result to its caller. It checks that result through the assertion instead. Its empty parentheses mean no test arguments are supplied here. The braces enclose the two statements that perform the experiment.

void addOne_four_returnsFive() {
    int actual = Numbers.addOne(4);
    assertEquals(5, actual);
}

flow.title: Mark the method with @Test
flow.html:
JUnit needs to know which methods are tests. Put the annotation @Test immediately before this method. An annotation is a marker attached to the following declaration. The method name can describe the case; it does not need a special test prefix. The marker identifies this ordinary Jupiter test.

@Test
void addOne_four_returnsFive() {
    assertEquals(5, Numbers.addOne(4));
}

flow.title: Enclose the test method in a class
flow.html:
A Java class body contains its methods. The outer braces below belong to NumbersTest; the inner braces belong to its test method. NumbersTest is our test class. Numbers is the separate supplied production class being called. Keeping those names distinct helps you see which code performs the operation and which code checks it.

class NumbersTest {
    @Test
    void addOne_four_returnsFive() {
        assertEquals(5, Numbers.addOne(4));
    }
}

flow.title: Import the Test annotation
flow.html:
Just as BigInteger needed a library import, the annotation type Test comes from a library. This import makes JUnit Jupiter’s Test available by its short name. Put it above the class declaration. The project must already include JUnit; writing an import selects a name from the library rather than installing the library.

import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

flow.title: Import the assertion methods
flow.html:
The assertion methods belong to the JUnit class Assertions. A static import lets you call those methods by their short names, such as assertEquals. The star means all its static members are available by name. This line is separate from importing Test: one supplies the annotation name, while the other supplies assertion names.

import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.*;

flow.title: Assemble the complete file
flow.html:
Now combine the pieces you have already written. Imports go first, followed by the test class. Inside the class is the marked void method, and inside that method is the assertion. This complete file assumes Numbers is supplied in the same package and JUnit Jupiter is available in the project.

import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.*;

class NumbersTest {
    @Test
    void addOne_four_returnsFive() {
        assertEquals(5, Numbers.addOne(4));
    }
}

flow.title: Keep the test’s return type separate
flow.html:
The method under test can return int while its test returns void. A Jupiter test succeeds by finishing without a failed assertion or unexpected failure; it does not report success by returning true. The ordinary test methods used here are nonstatic and not private, with no parameters. Use the plain void header you have practised.

@Test
void addOne_four_returnsFive() {

flow.title: Compare String contents
flow.html:
The equality assertion also works with Strings. It uses String’s content equality, so the expected text belongs first and the observed text second. This checks the actual letters, not just their length. The supplied method Names.label() promises the String Ada; its implementation is hidden because the promise supplies our expected value.

String actual = Names.label();
assertEquals("Ada", actual);

flow.title: Match the expected object type
flow.html:
BigInteger equality compares BigInteger numeric values. Construct the expected value as BigInteger too. For this example, Amounts.addOne(BigInteger amount) returns a BigInteger one greater than its argument. The literal 5 alone is an int; it is not a BigInteger expected value, even though both can describe the number five.

BigInteger actual = Amounts.addOne(BigInteger.valueOf(4));
assertEquals(BigInteger.valueOf(5), actual);

flow.title: Assert that a boolean is true
flow.html:
Use assertTrue when the promised observation is true. It takes a boolean expression, not an expected/actual pair. Counter starts at zero, and its supplied boolean method isZero returns true exactly at zero. The call already answers the yes-or-no question, so put that returned boolean directly inside the assertion.

Counter counter = new Counter();
assertTrue(counter.isZero());

flow.title: Assert that a boolean is false
flow.html:
Use assertFalse when the contract requires the boolean observation to be false. It also takes one boolean expression. After set changes Counter’s count to 3, isZero should answer false. The assertion name expresses the required answer, while the expression inside supplies the actual answer.

Counter counter = new Counter();
counter.set(3);
assertFalse(counter.isZero());

flow.title: Assert an absent reference
flow.html:
Use assertNull when the contract promises no object. The supplied method Names.nickname(String name) returns null for an unknown name. The assertion checks that the actual reference is null. It does not ask whether a String is empty: an empty String is still an existing object.

String actual = Names.nickname("Unknown");
assertNull(actual);

flow.title: Assert that a reference exists
flow.html:
Use assertNotNull when you need to check that an object was returned. It says nothing about that object’s contents. Suppose Names.nickname promises a non-null String for Ada but does not specify its exact text. Presence is the justified check here; inventing a particular nickname would add a requirement the contract does not contain.

String actual = Names.nickname("Ada");
assertNotNull(actual);

flow.title: Separate identity from equal state
flow.html:
Two variables can refer to the very same object. Assigning first to alias copies the reference; it does not create a second Counter. By contrast, another new expression creates a distinct Counter. Both Counters start at zero, so matching counts do not prove they are the same object. Identity means the same particular object.

Counter first = new Counter();
Counter alias = first;
Counter other = new Counter();

flow.title: Assert the same object
flow.html:
Use assertSame(expected, actual) for an identity promise. The supplied static method Counters.identity(Counter value) promises to return the exact object it receives. A newly created Counter with the same count would violate that promise. Comparing the returned reference with the original is the observation that distinguishes those outcomes.

Counter original = new Counter();
Counter actual = Counters.identity(original);
assertSame(original, actual);

flow.title: Assert distinct objects
flow.html:
Use assertNotSame when two references must designate different objects. The supplied static method Counters.fresh() promises a newly created zero-valued Counter on every call. Two calls may return equal counts, but they must not return one shared Counter. Not-same checks their identity; it does not check either count.

Counter first = Counters.fresh();
Counter second = Counters.fresh();
assertNotSame(first, second);

flow.title: Compare array contents
flow.html:
Use assertArrayEquals to compare array lengths and corresponding elements. Ordinary assertEquals on int arrays does not perform this element-by-element check. The supplied Copies.copy(int[] input) promises a new array with the same elements in the same order. Start by checking its contents using an independently written expected array.

int[] actual = Copies.copy(new int[]{2, 5});
assertArrayEquals(new int[]{2, 5}, actual);

flow.title: Check two different promised properties
flow.html:
An array copy has two separate obligations here: preserve contents and return a distinct array. An array-content assertion checks the first. An identity assertion checks the second. Neither alone establishes both. Combining these already learned assertions is useful because a faulty method could simply return its input and still have exactly the required contents.

int[] input = new int[]{2, 5};
int[] actual = Copies.copy(input);
assertArrayEquals(new int[]{2, 5}, actual);
assertNotSame(input, actual);

Use a double variable for that result. This introduces the numeric type first; the next step will explain why some decimal computations need a tolerance.

flow.title: Define an acceptable difference
flow.html:
Many decimal fractions cannot be represented exactly by a double, so arithmetic may produce a tiny rounding difference. An absolute tolerance is the largest allowed distance between expected and actual. Choose it from the accuracy requirement, not merely to make a failure disappear. With a tolerance of 0.001, a difference of 0.0004 is acceptable; 0.02 is not.

The example allows only a very small rounding difference for 0.1 plus 0.2. Use the accuracy limit required by your own contract when writing a test.

assertEquals(0.3, actual, 0.000000001);

title: Test a change of state
summary: Prepare one Counter, perform one target operation, and check the state afterward.
goals: Separate setup, target action, and observation in a state-changing test.
Give each test a fresh, independent fixture.
Use a class field and @BeforeEach without hiding the fixture in a local variable.
setup: Prepare one Counter, perform one target operation, and check the state afterward.

flow.title: Observe a void operation afterward
flow.html:
Return to Counter. Its no-argument constructor starts at zero, set replaces its count, and get reads it. Now add one supplied operation: void increment() increases the stored count by one. Like set, it returns no value. Call increment first, then use get to observe whether the count changed as promised.

Counter counter = new Counter();
counter.set(4);
counter.increment();
int actual = counter.get();

flow.title: Arrange the starting state
flow.html:
Arrange means preparing everything the case needs before the target operation. To test increment from four, create a fresh Counter and set its count to four. Those statements are setup for this particular experiment. A set call could be the target of another test; its role here is to establish increment’s starting state.

Counter counter = new Counter();
counter.set(4);

flow.title: Act on the arranged object
flow.html:
Act means performing the operation this case is designed to check. Here it is one increment call on the arranged Counter. Do not create a replacement object between setup and action: it would lose the prepared count. Keeping the action explicit helps you identify exactly which call the resulting observation is evidence about.

counter.increment();

flow.title: Assert the state after acting
flow.html:
Assert means comparing an observation with the contract’s expected result. After one increment from four, get should return five. The assertion reads the same object after the action. Checking before increment would describe only the setup; trying to compare increment’s return would fail because void supplies no value.

counter.increment();
assertEquals(5, counter.get());

flow.title: Assemble arrange, act, assert
flow.html:
The three roles form one test: arrange the starting state, act once, then assert the result. Comments can label the roles without changing execution. The method name describes the starting condition and expected outcome. All syntax here is familiar; the new skill is organizing those pieces so the test’s purpose is easy to read.

@Test
void increment_fromFour_becomesFive() {
    // Arrange
    Counter counter = new Counter();
    counter.set(4);
    // Act
    counter.increment();
    // Assert
    assertEquals(5, counter.get());
}

flow.title: Give each test its own fixture
flow.html:
A fixture is the object and state prepared for a test. A fresh Counter inside each test keeps the cases independent. One case’s mutation cannot become another case’s accidental setup. Tests should not require a particular running order. The two local variables below have the same name but refer to objects created separately for their own tests.

@Test
void newCounter_startsAtZero() {
    Counter counter = new Counter();
    assertEquals(0, counter.get());
}

@Test
void increment_fromZero_becomesOne() {
    Counter counter = new Counter();
    counter.increment();
    assertEquals(1, counter.get());
}

flow.title: Store a fixture in a class field
flow.html:
A variable declared directly inside a class is a field. Methods of that object can use it. A variable declared inside a method is local to that method. A reference field such as counter starts as null until assigned an object. Below, makeCounter assigns the class field rather than creating a new local variable.

class CounterTest {
    Counter counter;

    void makeCounter() {
        counter = new Counter();
    }
}

flow.title: Assign the field without hiding it
flow.html:
Repeating the type inside a method declares a new local variable. If that local variable has the same name as a field, it hides the field within that method. The field stays unchanged. To initialize the existing counter field, assign to counter without repeating Counter. This small syntax difference determines which variable receives the object.

Counter counter;

void makeCounter() {
    counter = new Counter();
}

flow.title: Limit a fixture field with private
flow.html:
The keyword private limits access to a member from outside its enclosing class. Our tests can still use their own private fixture field. This differs from the ordinary Jupiter test method, which must not be private. Use private for the field below while keeping the already learned plain void header for the test method.

}

flow.title: Prepare the field with @BeforeEach
flow.html:
JUnit can run a setup method before every test method. Mark that void method with @BeforeEach and import the annotation. The name setUp is descriptive; the marker controls its role. Assign a new Counter to the existing field each time. Then every test begins with its own newly prepared zero-count fixture.

import org.junit.jupiter.api.BeforeEach;
@BeforeEach
void setUp() {
    counter = new Counter();
}

flow.title: Follow the setup lifecycle
flow.html:
BeforeEach runs again for the next test. If one test increments counter, the next setup assigns a fresh zero-count Counter before the next test starts. The second test should therefore reason from the setup promise, not from another test’s final state. We do not need to predict which test runs first to explain this fixture.

flow.html:
Combine the pieces into a complete file. The field names the fixture, BeforeEach prepares it, and the test arranges the particular starting count before acting and asserting. The setup gives every case a fresh object; each test remains responsible for any extra state its own case needs. All imports belong above the class.

    void setUp() {

    @Test
    void increment_fromFour_becomesFive() {
        counter.set(4);
        counter.increment();
        assertEquals(5, counter.get());
    }
}

title: Understand what the result tells you
summary: Separate invalid Java, missing tests, failed comparisons, unexpected exceptions, and weak passing checks.
goals: Identify whether a problem occurs at compilation, test discovery, or execution.

flow.title: Compilation comes before execution
flow.html:
Java must compile before a test can run. Compilation checks syntax and type rules, not whether addOne fulfills its promise. A missing semicolon makes the source invalid, so no assertion result exists yet. Repair the syntax first, then execute the test to learn about its behavior. These are different stages of the work.

int actual = Numbers.addOne(4);
assertEquals(5, actual);

flow.title: A wrong argument type prevents compilation
flow.html:
A call must fit the method’s parameter types. Numbers supplies only static int addOne(int number). The quoted text "4" is a String, so it cannot fill this int parameter. The compiler rejects the call before Numbers executes. This is not evidence that the implementation returned the wrong answer; no call has run.

Numbers.addOne("4");

flow.title: The assertion has parameter types too
flow.html:
JUnit calls also obey Java’s type rules. assertTrue takes a boolean, while Numbers.addOne returns an int. Putting the int result inside assertTrue does not mean “the result is correct”; it is a mismatched argument. To check an exact numeric result, use the equality assertion with the independently expected int first.

assertEquals(5, Numbers.addOne(4));

flow.title: A compiled method may not be discovered
flow.html:
After compilation, JUnit discovers the test methods to run. In the ordinary Jupiter form used here, @Test marks the method. A descriptive name alone does not do that. The following method compiles but is an ordinary unmarked method, so Jupiter does not discover it as a test. No discovered tests is different from tests that ran and passed.

class NumbersTest {
    void addOne_four_returnsFive() {
        assertEquals(5, Numbers.addOne(4));
    }
}

flow.title: A reached comparison can fail
flow.html:
An assertion failure means the test reached a check and the observation did not satisfy it. Suppose addOne’s contract says plus one, but its implementation adds two. For input four, actual becomes six. The assertion expects five and reports the mismatch. The source can compile even though its behavior violates the contract.

static int addOne(int number) {
    return number + 2;
}
assertEquals(5, Numbers.addOne(4));

flow.title: Check the test’s expected result too
flow.html:
A failed assertion does not by itself prove that production code is wrong. The test may have encoded the wrong expectation. Re-read the contract before changing either side. If addOne correctly adds one, input four must produce five; a test expecting six is faulty. Fixing the expectation must follow the promise, not simply copy whichever value happened to appear.

static int addOne(int number) {
    return number + 1;
}
assertEquals(6, Numbers.addOne(4));

flow.title: An unexpected exception can stop the test
flow.html:
A test can stop before reaching its assertion. Calling length on null throws NullPointerException because no String object exists to receive the call. The fragment is type-correct Java: null can be stored in a String reference. This is an execution failure from an unexpected exception, not a reached comparison reporting unequal expected and actual values.

String text = null;
int actual = text.length();
assertEquals(0, actual);

flow.title: A discovered empty test can pass
flow.html:
A marked void test with an empty body can run and pass: it performs no failing operation. That green result contains no observation about addOne. It differs from a missing @Test marker because this test really was discovered and executed. To make it useful, add a call and an assertion tied to the contract.

@Test
void addOne_four_returnsFive() {
}

flow.title: Avoid comparing an observation with itself
flow.html:
An assertion can run and still provide no useful check of the promise. Comparing actual with itself always accepts this int value, even when addOne returns the wrong number. The missing piece is an independent expectation. Replace one copy of the observation with the answer calculated from the contract, keeping the observation second.

int actual = Numbers.addOne(4);
assertEquals(actual, actual);

flow.title: A weaker true statement may miss the defect
flow.html:
A passing assertion proves only its stated property for that execution. If addOne(4) incorrectly returns six, the condition actual > 0 is still true. Positivity is weaker than the promised exact result five. The test is valid Java and really checks something, but its observation is too loose to distinguish this defect from correct behavior.

int actual = Numbers.addOne(4);
assertTrue(actual > 0);

flow.title: Classify before repairing
flow.html:
Classify the outcome before changing code. Check compilation, then test discovery, then execution. During execution, distinguish a reached assertion from an exception that stops the test earlier. For a passing test, inspect exactly which promised property its checks establish.
